report.summary: Specification mining (Daikon, Texada) reports >90% precision for simple invariants; NL-to-assertion (Toradocu, Jdoctor) ~70-85% precision for comment-code consistency. Disagreements: soundness vs completeness, static vs dynamic. Recommend LLM-based extraction + runtime assertions. Measure precision internally.
risks: LLM may hallucinate specifications, leading to false assertions
Dynamic mining limited to observed paths
Runtime monitoring may introduce performance overhead
Literature precision may not transfer to Python codebases
todos: Build LLM-based extraction: parse docstrings into formal assertions using few-shot prompts
Implement lightweight runtime checks for 'never writes X' and atomicity using decorators
Run on sample of 100 docstrings, manually label, compute precision/recall
Iterate on prompt engineering and assertion generation

handoff.suggestion: Use existing LLM routing to call a model trained to extract formal assertions from docstrings. Combine with a runtime monitor (e.g., Python's settrace or context managers) to verify 'never writes X' and atomicity properties. Start by generating assertions for a small set of critical functions and manually verify correctness.

name: q29-docstring-drift-detection
question: Detecting docstrings that promise guarantees the implementation does not provide -- atomicity, fail-closed behaviour, 'never writes X'. What automated techniques exist (specification mining, NL-to-assertion, contract inference), and what precision do they report on real codebases?
